The *Times* was founded as the conservative *New-York Daily Times* in 1851, and came to national recognition in the 1870s with its aggressive coverage of corrupt politician [Boss Tweed](/wiki/William_M._Tweed "William M. Tweed"). Following the [Panic of 1893](/wiki/Panic_of_1893 "Panic of 1893"), *[Chattanooga Times](/wiki/Chattanooga_Times "Chattanooga Times")* publisher [Adolph Ochs](/wiki/Adolph_Ochs "Adolph Ochs") gained a controlling interest in the company. In 1935, Ochs was succeeded by his son-in-law, [Arthur Hays Sulzberger](/wiki/Arthur_Hays_Sulzberger "Arthur Hays Sulzberger"), who began a push into European news. Sulzberger's son [Arthur Ochs Sulzberger](/wiki/Arthur_Ochs_Sulzberger "Arthur Ochs Sulzberger") became publisher in 1963, adapting to a changing newspaper industry and introducing radical changes. *The New York Times* was involved in the landmark 1964 [U.S. Supreme Court](/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") case *[New York Times Co. v. Sullivan](/wiki/New_York_Times_Co._v._Sullivan "New York Times Co. v. Sullivan")*, which restricted the ability of public officials to sue the media for [defamation](/wiki/Defamation "Defamation").

In 1971, *The New York Times* published the *[Pentagon Papers](/wiki/Pentagon_Papers "Pentagon Papers")*, an internal [Department of Defense](/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") document detailing the [United States's historical involvement](/wiki/United_States_in_the_Vietnam_War "United States in the Vietnam War") in the [Vietnam War](/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"), despite pushback from then-president [Richard Nixon](/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon"). In the landmark decision *[New York Times Co. v. United States](/wiki/New_York_Times_Co._v._United_States "New York Times Co. v. Kingsbury spent his early years living in and around [Guelph](/wiki/Guelph "Guelph"), [Ontario](/wiki/Ontario "Ontario").[[1]](#cite_note-1) He comes from a musical family; his mother Birdie was a pianist and a music director and Parkwood Gardens Community church in Guelph, and Kingsbury sang in the church choir.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) His brother Brett is a professional classical pianist. After piano lessons as a child, Kingsbury stopped playing music until a friend of his mother gave him a guitar when he was fourteen. He began to teach himself to play and write music.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3) Kingsbury attended John F. Ross in Guelph[[4]](#cite_note-:2-4) where he began playing in bands when he was sixteen.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3) Christian rock was an early influence for Kingsbury,[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) especially the music of pioneering American Christian rock artist [Larry Norman](/wiki/Larry_Norman "Larry Norman").[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3) Kingsbury cites his later influences as [Pavement](/wiki/Pavement_(band) "Pavement (band)") and Palace and [Dinosaur Jr](/wiki/Dinosaur_Jr. "Dinosaur Jr.").[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3) He played with [Gentleman Reg](/wiki/Gentleman_Reg "Gentleman Reg") while in high school, only playing one show outside of Guelph.[[5]](#cite_note-:3-5)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Merlot_grapes_being_sorted_at_Chateau_Kirwan.jpg/250px-Merlot_grapes_being_sorted_at_Chateau_Kirwan.jpg)](/wiki/File:Merlot_grapes_being_sorted_at_Chateau_Kirwan.jpg)

[Merlot](/wiki/Merlot "Merlot") grapes being sorted at [Château Kirwan](/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Kirwan "Château Kirwan")

The red grapes in the Bordeaux vineyard are Merlot (62% by area), Cabernet Sauvignon (25%), Cabernet Franc (12%) and a small amount of Petit Verdot, Malbec and Carménère (1% in total). The white grapes are Sémillon (54% by area), Sauvignon blanc (36%), Muscadelle (7%) and a small amount of Ugni blanc, Colombard and Folle blanche (3% in total).[[3]](#cite_note-Bordeaux_Figures-3) Because of the generally humid Bordeaux climate, a variety of pests can cause a problem for the *[vigneron](/wiki/Winemaker "Winemaker")*. In the past, this was counteracted by the widespread use of pesticides, although the use of natural methods has recently been gaining in popularity. The vines are generally [trained](/wiki/Vine_training "Vine training") in either single or double guyot. Hand-picking is preferred by most of the prestigious châteaux, but machine-harvesting is popular in other places.[[14]](#cite_note-Brook_36-74-14)

Italian campaign (World War II) :: Strategic background :: chunk_0006
The British, especially the [Prime Minister](/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom"), [Winston Churchill](/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill"), advocated their traditional naval-based peripheral strategy. Even with a large army, but greater naval power, the traditional British answer against a continental enemy was to fight as part of a coalition, blockading with their navy and mount small peripheral operations designed to gradually weaken the enemy. The United States, with the larger [U.S. Army](/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army"), favoured a more direct method of fighting the main force of the [German Army](/wiki/German_Army_(1935%E2%80%931945) "German Army (1935–1945)") in [northwestern Europe](/wiki/Western_Front_(World_War_II) "Western Front (World War II)"). The ability to launch such a campaign depended on first winning the [Battle of the Atlantic](/wiki/Battle_of_the_Atlantic "Battle of the Atlantic").

The strategic disagreement was fierce, with the U.S. service chiefs arguing for an invasion of France as early as possible, while their British counterparts advocated a policy centred on operations in the [Mediterranean](/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea"). There was even pressure from some [Latin American](/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America") countries to stage an invasion of Spain, which, under [Francisco Franco](/wiki/Francisco_Franco "Francisco Franco"), was friendly to the Axis nations, although not a participant in the war.[[41]](#cite_note-54) The American staff believed that a full-scale invasion of France at the earliest possible time was required to end the war in Europe, and that no operations should be undertaken that might delay that effort.

The vast majority of Pennsylvania's population is made up of Whites, Blacks, Hispanics, and Asian Americans. Harvard is governed by a combination of its [Board of Overseers](/wiki/Harvard_Board_of_Overseers "Harvard Board of Overseers") and the [President and Fellows of Harvard College](/wiki/President_and_Fellows_of_Harvard_College "President and Fellows of Harvard College"), which is also known as the Harvard Corporation. These two bodies, in turn, appoint the [president of Harvard University](/wiki/President_of_Harvard_University "President of Harvard University").[[93]](#cite_note-94)

There are 16,000 staff and faculty,[[94]](#cite_note-95) including 2,400 professors, lecturers, and instructors in the colleges proper,[[95]](#cite_note-96) plus another >10,400 academic appointments in affiliated teaching hospitals)[[96]](#cite_note-97)

As of 2025, Harvard differs radically from its peer universities in two important ways. First, Harvard does not make its governing statutes publicly available, meaning that members of the Harvard community interested in reform must first persuade the university to give them a copy of those documents. Second, Harvard does not have an [academic senate](/wiki/Academic_senate "Academic senate") like most of its peers, although it is currently attempting to create one.[[97]](#cite_note-Heller-98)

[Saturn](/wiki/Saturn "Saturn") has [292 moons](/wiki/Moons_of_Saturn "Moons of Saturn") with known orbits announced; 66 of them have received permanent designations, and 63 have been named. Most of them are quite small. Seven moons are large enough to be in [hydrostatic equilibrium](/wiki/Hydrostatic_equilibrium "Hydrostatic equilibrium"), including [Titan](/wiki/Titan_(moon) "Titan (moon)"), the second largest moon in the Solar System. Including these large moons, 24 of Saturn's moons are regular, and traditionally named after [Titans](/wiki/Titan_(mythology) "Titan (mythology)") or other figures associated with the mythological [Saturn](/wiki/Saturn_(mythology) "Saturn (mythology)"). The remaining moons are irregular, and classified by their orbital characteristics into [Inuit](/wiki/Saturn%27s_Inuit_group_of_satellites "Saturn's Inuit group of satellites"), [Norse](/wiki/Saturn%27s_Norse_group_of_satellites "Saturn's Norse group of satellites"), and [Gallic](/wiki/Saturn%27s_Gallic_group_of_satellites "Saturn's Gallic group of satellites") groups, and their names are chosen from the corresponding mythologies the groups are named after. The [rings of Saturn](/wiki/Rings_of_Saturn "Rings of Saturn") are made up of icy objects ranging in size from one centimetre to hundreds of metres, each of which is on its own orbit about the planet. Thus, a precise number of Saturnian moons cannot be given, as there is no objective boundary between the countless small anonymous objects that form Saturn's ring system and the larger objects that have been named as moons. At least 150 "[moonlets](/wiki/Moonlet "Moonlet")" embedded in the rings have been detected by the disturbance they create in the surrounding ring material, though this is thought to be only a small sample of the total population of such objects.
